cards.text: This psalm is from Asaph, a Levite musician who led worship in David's day (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). It's written for the choirmaster. Asaph opens with a call to God's people, and friend, it is NOT a quiet one.

cards.question: Asaph opens by calling God's people to sing for joy to God.

cards.text: And he wants the WHOLE band: a song, the tambourine, the harp and the lyre. I sing to my ovens every morning, and not ONE of them has ever asked for an encore.

cards.question: Next Asaph calls for the ram's horn, and he ties it to the calendar. When should it sound?

answers.text: At the New Moon and the full moon
On the first day of the harvest

cards.question: Asaph gives a reason for all this noise on the feast day. What is it?

answers.text: God made it a statute for Israel

cards.text: Asaph says God set it up as a testimony for Joseph. It reaches back to a land Israel knew all too well.

cards.question: This testimony for Joseph goes back to the land of ___.

cards.text: Then the singer hears an unfamiliar language, and God begins to speak. He's looking back at His people carrying heavy loads.

cards.question: God remembers the burden on His people's shoulder. What does He say He did about it?

cards.text: You know the one-trip-from-the-car move, every bag on both arms, fingers turning PURPLE? Now picture all of it lifted off, because God says their hands were freed from the basket.
And God keeps remembering. His people called out to Him in distress.

cards.question: When His people called out in distress, God says He ___ them.
God says He answered His people from a cloud of thunder.

cards.text: Then God names a place: the waters of Meribah, where the people once quarreled over water (Exodus 17:1-7).

cards.question: What does God say happened at the waters of Meribah?

cards.text: Selah. Deep breath. Now God tells His people He's about to warn them, and I think you can hear His heart in it.

cards.question: God says He wishes His people would listen to Him.

cards.text: If only you would listen. Friend, I once ignored an oven timer for nine full minutes because I KNEW better, and the smoke alarm did NOT agree.

cards.question: God warns Israel about one thing that must never be among them. What is it?

cards.text: Then God reminds them who's talking: the LORD their God, who brought them up out of Egypt. And He says, "Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it."

cards.question: When God tells Israel to open wide their mouth so He can fill it, what is He offering?

answers.text: To give them what they need
To teach them a new song

cards.question: After an offer like that, God says His people listened and obeyed Him.
Israel won't listen to God. So what does God do?

answers.text: Gives them up to their stubborn hearts

cards.text: Oof. That one stings. But God isn't done, and here comes that wish again: if only His people would listen, if Israel would follow His ways.

cards.question: If Israel would follow His ways, God says He'd soon turn His hand against their ___.

cards.text: Then God talks about those who hate the LORD, and how they would act.

cards.question: God says those who hate the LORD would truly obey Him.

cards.text: And how does God finish this psalm? Not with enemies. With feeding His people.

cards.question: If only His people would listen, what does God say He would feed them?

cards.text: And with honey from the rock, God says He would satisfy them. Honey from a ROCK, friend. I've stared at plenty of rocks, and not one has ever handed me a thing.

findings.problem: "Then the singer hears an unfamiliar language, and God begins to speak" makes two claims the text doesn't support. First, it names the "I" of verse 5 as the singer, but the text leaves the speaker open. Second, it makes the hearing happen now, just before God speaks. The text places it "over the land of Egypt, where I heard an unfamiliar language," back when Joseph went out. Placing it in the present links the unfamiliar language to God's speech, a link the text leaves open.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong. Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "friends" is silly. God rewarding obedience by turning His hand against Israel's friends isn't believable, so it doesn't match the tone of the other answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The second half of Psalm 81:15, "and their doom would last forever," is never told on any card. Cards 11 and 12 cover only the feigned obedience, so the baker misses what the verse says happens to those who hate the LORD.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Most story cards are plain retelling with no humor or personality. In stop 1, cards 6, 8, 11 and 14 are flat, and card 10 is the only laugh after card 3. In stop 2, cards 1, 11 and 13 are flat. Across 14 story cards there are only four jokes (stop 1 cards 3 and 10, stop 2 cards 3 and 15), and the rest read like a pleasant narrator, not laugh-out-loud Papa Dorin.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
